title: HomoGCL: Rethinking Homophily in Graph Contrastive Learning

problem.claim: Graph contrastive learning commonly follows an augmenting-and-contrasting scheme, yet it can perform decently without augmentation.

gap.claim: The role of homophily in explaining graph contrastive learning's success without augmentation has not been explicitly leveraged.

contributions.claim: The authors argue that homophily plays a key role in the success of graph contrastive learning.
HomoGCL is a model-agnostic framework that expands the positive set using neighbor nodes with neighbor-specific significances.
HomoGCL introduces a stricter lower bound on the mutual information between raw node features and node embeddings in augmented views.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report multiple state-of-the-art results across six public datasets.
The authors report consistent notable performance improvements when HomoGCL is applied to various graph contrastive learning methods.
The authors report that HomoGCL can be combined with existing graph contrastive learning models in a plug-and-play manner with light extra computational overhead.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph contrastive learning is generally based on augmenting and contrasting.
Graph contrastive learning performs decently even without augmentation.
The authors analyze this phenomenon and identify homophily as a key factor.
HomoGCL expands the positive set with neighbor nodes weighted by neighbor-specific significance.

The method is theoretically motivated, plug-and-play, computationally light according to the authors, and experimentally reported to improve results across datasets and graph contrastive learning methods.

source_observation.claim: Graph contrastive learning can perform decently without augmentation, and homophily is argued to contribute to this behavior.

interpretation.claim: Native graph structure may provide useful positive relationships that reduce the need for aggressive augmentation.

application.claim: When designing graph self-supervised learning methods, evaluate whether neighborhood structure can define or expand positive sets.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this approach applies equally across graphs with different homophily characteristics.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the six datasets, evaluation metrics, or baseline models.
The abstract does not report numerical performance gains, lower-bound details, or measured computational overhead.
